stops.name: Roncevaux, the Oliphant blown at last
stops.campa: The Peers are falling; sixty men stand of twenty thousand. Now Roland says he will sound the horn, and it is Oliver who refuses him in bitter grief. Too late, the blood is spilt. Archbishop Turpin parts them: the horn cannot save them, but Charles will come to avenge and bury them. Then Roland sets the oliphant to his mouth and blows with such force that the veins of his temples burst; the bright blood springs from his mouth. Thirty leagues away the sound reaches Charles: 'Our men give battle,' says the king. Ganelon answers that it is nothing. The mountains carry the horn three times.
stops.quote: Rollant ad mis l'olifan a sa buche, / Empeint le ben, par grant vertut le sunet... / Par mi la buche en salt fors li cler sancs, / De sun cervel le temple en est rumpant.

stops.name: Roncevaux, Durendal against the stone
stops.campa: Roland, dying, feels his sight go and thinks of the sword. Durendal must not fall to the pagans: in its golden hilt are sealed a tooth of Saint Peter, blood of Saint Basil, hair of Saint Denis, a piece of the raiment of the Virgin. Ten times he strikes the dark stone; the steel grates and will not break, will not even notch, and springs back toward heaven. He laments over it as over a bride: the conquests they made together, the emperor's beard, sweet France. Unable to break it he lays himself upon it, sword and oliphant beneath his body, so that even his corpse guards them.
stops.quote: E! Durendal, cum es bele e clere e blanche! / Cuntre soleill si luises e reflambes!

stops.name: Roncevaux, Roland dies facing Spain
stops.campa: He goes at a run (dying, he still runs) up under a pine on a little hill, and lies down on the green grass face toward Spain, sword and horn beneath him, so that Charles and all his host shall say he died a conqueror, his face to the enemy. He confesses his sins, beats his breast, and holds up his right glove to God as a vassal returns his fief. Saint Gabriel and Saint Michael of the Peril come down with cherubim and carry the count's soul into Paradise. On the field around him twenty thousand Franks lie dead, and not one with his wounds behind.
stops.quote: Desuz un pin i est alet curant, / Sur l'erbe verte s'i est culchet adenz, / Desuz lui met s'espee e l'olifan, / Turnat sa teste vers la paiene gent.

stops.name: Roncevaux, the emperor turns back too late
stops.campa: Charles comes back through the pass with the host at the gallop, and for him God works the great wonder: the sun stands still in heaven, halted so the Franks may hunt the pagans into the Ebro before dark. But at Roncevaux there is nothing left to save. The emperor rides among the dead calling for his nephew, for the archbishop, for Oliver, and no one answers; he finds Roland under the pine and faints upon the body, tearing his white beard. A hundred thousand Franks weep with him. The annals say drily that the baggage was lost and the enemy scattered beyond vengeance.
stops.quote: Carles escriet: 'U estes vos, bels nies? / U est l'arcevesque? E li quens Oliver?'

stops.name: Blaye, the three biers in Saint-Romain
stops.campa: The emperor has the hearts of Roland, Oliver and Turpin wrapped in silk and their bodies borne down through Gascony; the Gironde is crossed in great ships, and at Blaye, in the basilica of Saint-Romain, the three lords are laid in white sarcophagi. There the song leaves them: la gisent li baron, there lie the barons. For a thousand years pilgrims on the Compostela road will turn aside at Blaye to stand over Roland, and at Bordeaux, on the altar of Saint-Seurin, the oliphant itself is laid up, filled with gold. Charles rides north to learn the Saxons have risen the moment his back was turned.
stops.quote: En blancs sarcous fait metre les seignurs / A Seint Romain: la gisent li baron.

stops.name: The Suntel hills, the host cut down among the trees
stops.campa: Widukind is back from the Danes and Saxony burns again. A Frankish force under the king's chamberlain, marshal and counts, jealous of sharing glory, charges up into the Suntel hills without order, each man riding as fast as his horse can carry him, as if racing rather than attacking. In the trees the Saxons close around them. Two of the king's officers, four counts and twenty noblemen die with the men who followed them, the worst Frankish blood spilled in the whole thirty years' war. The news comes to Charles and something in the king goes cold and exact.

stops.name: Verden on the Aller, the terrible number
stops.campa: Charles comes into Saxony with the anger of a king and a bereaved lord, and at Verden, where the Aller meets the Weser, the Saxon nobles deliver up the men of the rebellion, all but Widukind, who is gone again over the Elbe. The canon writes the number without flinching, and this register keeps it as written: four thousand five hundred Saxons, handed over, and beheaded in one day by the river. Then the king goes to winter quarters. The Aller runs to the sea. The chronicle passes to the next year's business, and the reader hears in the silence the sound the axes made from morning until dark.
stops.quote: He had as many as four thousand five hundred of them, who had been handed over, beheaded in one day at the place called Verden on the river Aller.

stops.name: The Eresburg, the king winters inside Saxony
stops.campa: For the first time Charles does not go home when the season turns: he keeps Christmas and then Easter at the Eresburg, wife and children with him, holding the winter itself as a conquered province. From the rock where the Irminsul's treasure was carried off, he sends columns out along the frozen rivers, burning the war out of the land month by month. It is the strategy of a man who has understood that Saxony cannot be defeated in summers; it must be inhabited. In the spring the assembly meets at Paderborn, and the roads of Saxony lie open in every direction.

stops.name: Attigny, Widukind baptized; the emperor his godfather
stops.campa: Worn down at last, Widukind asks for pledges, and the king sends them; and the man who burned the churches of the border for thirteen years crosses into Francia and comes to the royal villa of Attigny. There he is baptized, and Charles himself lifts his great enemy from the font, receiving him as a godson and honoring him with magnificent gifts. The war-leader of the old gods goes down into the water and comes up a Frank in white. The annals report that Saxony was then wholly subdued, and the register lets the sentence stand with its whole cost inside it: the pillar, the Aller, the font.
stops.quote: Then Widukind and Abbio came with their companions to Attigny, and there they were baptized, and the lord king raised Widukind from the font.

stops.name: Ingelheim, Tassilo shorn
stops.campa: At the palace of Ingelheim the assembly sits in judgment on Tassilo, duke of the Bavarians, cousin of the king, last of the Agilolfings. The charge is old and cold: harisliz, desertion of the host of Pepin thirty years before, warmed over with his Lombard wife's intrigues and dealings with the Avars. His own men accuse him. The Franks condemn him to death, and Charles, merciful as a door closing, commutes it: the duke is tonsured and sent into a monastery, his sons likewise, his duchy dissolved into the realm. Bavaria is folded in without a battle. The last of the old ducal houses ends under the scissors.

stops.name: Regensburg, the Avar war launched
stops.campa: From Regensburg on the Danube the king moves against the Avars, the horse-lords of Pannonia who have sat two centuries on the plunder of the Balkans behind their rings of earthwork. Before the host crosses the Enns, three days of litanies, fasting and masses are decreed: the whole army praying itself clean for a holy war. Then the columns move down both banks of the Danube with a fleet between them. The Avar khagans abandon their forward walls without a fight; the Franks march to the Raab through a country that empties before them like a tide going out.

stops.name: The Fossa Carolina, the canal between the seas
stops.campa: The king conceives a work no Caesar finished: to join the Rhine to the Danube, the Ocean to the Black Sea, by a canal between the Rezat and the Altmuehl, so that fleets may pass from the North Sea to the Avar war. Thousands of men dig through the autumn; the king comes in person and stays on the works. But rain without end turns the spoil to porridge, the marshy ground gives back by night what is dug by day, and the great trench is abandoned, a scar of water in the Franconian fields, dreaming of ships.
